name: Akoumé
subtitle: Akoumé is the Togolese name for tô, a thick cooked paste of cereal flour (millet, sorghum, maize, cassava or a mix) stirred into boiling water.

facts.label: Name
facts.value: Tô, a millet paste, is called akoumé in Togo.

facts.label: What it is
facts.value: A staple dish in Mali, Burkina Faso, Benin and Togo.

facts.label: Main ingredient
facts.value: Made from millet, sorghum, maize or cassava flour, or a mix of them, and water.

facts.label: Main ingredient
facts.value: Maize is the staple food in Togo.

facts.label: How often it is eaten
facts.value: It is often eaten every day, as rice is in Asia.

facts.label: How it is eaten
facts.value: It is eaten with a sauce made with vegetables, meat or chicken.

facts.label: How it is cooked
facts.value: It is cooked in unsalted water; the sauce supplies the seasoning.

facts.label: Origin
facts.value: Tô is said to be of Bambara origin.

parts.text: Akoumé is the Togolese name for tô, a thick cooked paste of cereal flour (millet, sorghum, maize, cassava or a mix) stirred into boiling water. It is a staple in Mali, Burkina Faso, Benin and Togo, said to be of Bambara origin, and maize is the staple grain in Togo.
It is often eaten daily, with a sauce of vegetables, meat or chicken; the paste is cooked without salt and the sauce gives it flavour.

blocks.title: Tô (Akoumé)
blocks.sub: One version of the dish, as given by Afrik.com; the steps are summarised in our own words. Recipes differ from cook to cook.
blocks.note: The source gives 30 minutes in total for preparation and cooking. It is the publisher's general tô recipe, not a specifically Togolese one.

ingredients.name: millet, sorghum, maize or cassava flour, or a mix

steps.text: Bring the water to the boil, without salt.
Put the flour in a bowl and work in about three-quarters of a litre of the boiling water, a little at a time, to make a paste.
Move the paste to a pot over low heat and keep adding the remaining boiling water bit by bit, stirring all the time so it neither sticks nor forms lumps.
Keep stirring until the paste is thick, adding more boiling water if needed; it is done when it comes away from the sides of the pot.
Shape portions by hand and serve each with meat, chicken or fish in a sauce.
